This patient presented with typical clinical features of the SMS with antiGADAb, but the illness progressed relentlessly over eight years and a supranuclear gaze paresis developed.

Five years after the illness began, the patient developed ileus and a bacterial overgrowth syndrome. Three years later, a prolonged episode of ileus was complicated by metabolic acidosis and delirium. There was no evidence of diabetes mellitus. Spasms continued, and were accompanied by generalised muscular rigidity, a fine tremor of extremities, extensor posturing and profuse sweating. There was a supranuclear paresis of vertical (predominantly downward) gaze, brisk flexor withdrawal reflexes of both legs, and rigidity of the abdominal wall and erector spinae muscles.

extractions.quote:
This patient presented with typical clinical features of the SMS with antiGADAb, but the illness progressed relentlessly over eight years and a supranuclear gaze paresis developed. This development and the post mortem finding of extensive, perivascular lymphocyte cuffing at multiple levels throughout the central nervous system is typical of PER. The patient was included in the original report of Solimena et al., 2 in which antibodies against gamma-aminobutyric-acid (GABA)-ergic neurones were demonstrated in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid in 60% of patients with a clinical diagnosis of stiff man syndrome. These observations prompted the suggestion of an autoimmune aetiology for SMS. 2, 3
Pathological examination of the central nervous system in patients with the SMS has yielded various findings. These have included normal or subtle change of uncertain significance, 1, 4–7 loss of anterior horn cells and spinal interneurones 8–13 and lymphocytic cuffing around brainstem and spinal cord meningeal vessels. 11, 12 In the six pathological studies of SMS with antiGADAb, perivascular lymphocytic cuffing was evident in three (present case 11), vacuolar degeneration of anterior horn cells was found in one 13 and in three, there was neuronal loss in the spinal cord (present case 14, 15).
The finding of encephalomyelitis, perivascular lymphocyte cuffing, loss of small and medium-sized ventral horn neurones, and demyelination sparing corticospinal tracts, in patients with axial rigidity and spasms, has been described previously as progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PER).
16–19 Two recent series of SMS included examples of PER. 12, 20 These were distinguished from SMS by additional extrapyramidal, brainstem, long tract and lower motor neurone signs and a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis, and a progressive course, in contrast to the more indolent course of SMS.
The antiGADAb status of most pathologically proven PER is not known, nor was it known in two cases of SMS with pathological evidence of encephalomyelitis. 10, 12 The present case is the third reported instance of an illness beginning as typical SMS with anti-GAD antibodies in which encephalomyelitis was subsequently found. The disease duration in these cases ranged from six to eight years, longer than most reported cases of PER. The late evolution of ocular motor signs in two of these cases suggests a change in the clinical picture from SMS to PER. These observations raise the question of whether there is clinical and pathological overlap between PER and SMS, and whether these conditions form a continuum of encephalomyelopathies, rather than representing distinct entities.
This patient presented with typical clinical features of the SMS with antiGADAb, but the illness progressed relentlessly over eight years and a supranuclear gaze paresis developed.
Antibodies to GAD were detected in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid.
Electromyography of the lower limbs demonstrated continuous motor unit activity, comprising units of normal morphology, despite attempted relaxation.
Baclofen, diazepam and vigabatrin produced some improvement in spasms and mobility but this was not sustained.
Extensive investigations including biochemical and haematological screens, brain and spinal cord imaging, and cerebrospinal fluid examination were normal.
There was no weakness, sensory loss, sphincteric disturbance or visual symptoms.
Antibodies to GAD were detected in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid.
